situation:
You are the guest information manager at LANTERN ROW MUSIC HALL, a nine-hundred-seat concert venue. The general manager (judge), who took over this year after two losing seasons, has asked you to recommend what the hall should do with its fan database, and to explain what information the hall would monitor once that decision is made.

The database has been built by hand for years. It records which shows each ticket buyer has attended, what they order at the bar and the kitchen counter, any food preference they mention, and a free-text note the door and floor staff type after every show. Three staff keep it current, and that takes part of every week.

That record is why the hall's service is what regulars describe to their friends. Bartenders know a returning guest's usual order, the kitchen stocks the vegan and non-alcoholic items a particular night's crowd actually buys, and the floor holds tables for people who always arrive late. Nothing about the music itself is unusual here; the treatment is.

The hall could let a national ticketing platform take the database over, and one has offered to. It would cut the weekly hours the three staff spend on it, produce clean segmented email lists, and forecast concession demand from genre averages across its own venues. It would also discard the free-text staff notes and the per-guest food preferences, because its fields do not hold them.

The hall could instead keep the database in-house, which preserves that treatment, but the hours stay on three staff who are needed on the floor during sold-out weeks, and there would still be no reliable forecast of what the bar and kitchen should stock. The general manager (judge) wants a recommendation and an account of what information the hall genuinely needs. The general manager (judge) will greet you, ask to hear your ideas, and will thank you after your presentation and questions.
judgeCharacterization:
You are the general manager (judge) at LANTERN ROW MUSIC HALL. Business background is the same as the situation above.

You came in this year to make the hall pay for itself again, and every standing cost is being looked at, the database among them. You want to hear a recommendation on what the hall should do with the database, what information it genuinely needs to make decisions, what the record says about what guests eat and drink, and how service would hold up on sold-out nights either way.

During the presentation you will ask the following questions:
judgeQuestions: Who ends up paying for the course you recommended?
Can we defend where that cost lands?
